50: Lectures five and six: everything becomes a grid of numbers. We look at images as matrices, audio as waveforms, the curse of dimensionality, and then bias and responsibility.
51: Here is the unifying idea. Three very different things, an image, a sound and a document, all end up as one representation: numbers. An image is a height by width grid of pixel values. A twenty eight by twenty eight grey photo is seven hundred eighty four numbers. A sound is one long list of amplitudes over time. One second at forty four thousand one hundred hertz is forty four thousand one hundred numbers. A document is counts across a vocabulary, so a twenty thousand word vocabulary gives twenty thousand numbers. Each of these is one row of a table, with hundreds or thousands of columns. That single fact creates both the power and the problem of the rest of this lecture.
52: An image is a matrix of brightness values. What the computer stores is just a grid of numbers. Zero is black, two fifty five is white, and everything in between is grey. The shape is height and width, and nothing else is stored. No edges, no objects, no meaning. Colour adds a third axis, height, width and three, for red, green and blue. So a one thousand twenty four by one thousand twenty four colour photo is three million, one hundred forty five thousand, seven hundred twenty eight numbers. One row, three million columns.
53: What does exploratory analysis look like for a folder of images? The first plot is the intensity histogram of pixel brightness. A spike at zero or two fifty five means clipped, blown out or blank images. Also check whether all images are the same size and orientation, how many images there are per class and whether the set is balanced, duplicates and near duplicates across train and test, and corrupt files, greyscale mixed into colour, or the wrong file type.
54: Audio is a list of numbers, sampled very fast. The sampling rate is how many measurements are taken per second: forty four thousand one hundred hertz for C D audio, and sixteen thousand hertz for speech. The bit depth is how finely each measurement is recorded. Sixteen bit gives sixty five thousand five hundred thirty six possible levels. Channels: mono is one list, stereo is two lists side by side. Ten seconds of speech at sixteen kilohertz is one hundred sixty thousand numbers. Nothing about pitch, words or speaker is stored. Every one of those has to be computed from this list.
55: Now a core machine learning idea: the curse of dimensionality. It explains why adding more features can make your data harder to learn from.
56: What is a dimension? In data, a dimension is simply a feature, one column of information about each item, like height, weight, age or income. A dataset with more columns has higher dimensionality, and that is where the trouble starts. Each new column is one more dimension.
57: As dimensions grow, space explodes. To keep the same ten points per side of resolution, the space you must fill grows exponentially. In one dimension you need ten points. In two dimensions you need one hundred. In three dimensions you need one thousand. That is an explosion, not a straight line.
58: The consequence is that your data becomes sparse. The amount of data almost never grows to match. So the same one thousand data points that densely filled a line now barely dust a cube. Models struggle because most of the space around any point is simply empty. On the left, low dimensions are dense and well covered. On the right, high dimensions have the same points but mostly empty space.
59: This also breaks distance. Many algorithms, like k nearest neighbours, rely on near versus far. In very high dimensions, that idea breaks down. The ratio of nearest to farthest neighbour distance approaches one as dimensions go to infinity. In plain terms, every point ends up looking almost equally close or far from every other point. The result: nearest neighbour stops being meaningful, and distance based models lose their edge.
60: A simple analogy: finding a friend, one dimension at a time. In one dimension, a street, your friend is somewhere on one road. Walk along it and you find them fast. In two dimensions, a park, they could be anywhere across an open field, and searching takes much longer. In three dimensions, a building, you add floors on top, and now you check rooms across many levels. Now imagine one hundred dimensions. In machine learning, one hundred or more features is normal, and the search space becomes almost impossible to cover.
61: How do we fight the curse? Four ways. One, feature selection: keep only the columns that actually help predict the outcome. Two, dimensionality reduction: techniques like P C A compress many features into a few meaningful ones. Three, regularisation: penalise model complexity so it does not chase noise in the extra dimensions. Four, more relevant data: more points help, but rarely enough to outrun exponential growth on their own.
62: The key takeaway: more features is not always better. Every added dimension expands the space exponentially, spreads your data thinner, and makes distance less meaningful. Choose fewer, more meaningful dimensions over simply adding more.
63: Here is the curse in one picture. Suppose you want ten measurements along every axis so that no region is unexplored. With two features, a hundred points is a comfortable grid. With six features, you need a million points, and six is a small dataset by today's standards. A twenty eight by twenty eight image has seven hundred eighty four features, and no dataset ever fills that space. Adding a column always adds information. It also always empties the space.
64: What goes wrong when the space is empty? One, everything is far from everything. Almost all pairs of points sit at a similar, large distance, so nearest neighbour stops being meaningful. Two, the data hugs the edges. Almost all of a high dimensional box's volume is near its surface, not its middle, so your typical point is not typical. Three, models overfit easily. With more columns than rows, a model can fit any pattern, including pure noise. Four, visualisation stops working. You can plot two dimensions, maybe three, and everything beyond that is inference, not sight. First responses: drop columns that carry nothing, build a few meaningful features by hand, and reduce dimensions with something like P C A before you model.
65: Now bias and ethics. Bias enters long before the model does. Stage one, the world: it is already unequal, and data records it faithfully. Stage two, collection: who got sampled and who was never reachable. Stage three, labelling: human judgement, fatigue and unclear guidelines. Stage four, modelling: the majority group drives the loss function. Stage five, deployment: decisions change behaviour, which changes the next dataset. And stage five feeds back into stage two. A system that stops lending to a neighbourhood stops collecting data about it. By the time you see a C S V, several of these decisions have already been made by someone else, usually undocumented.
66: Four ethical questions to ask of any dataset you did not collect. Consent: did these people agree to this use of their data, or only to some other use? Privacy: can an individual be re identified by combining columns, even after names are removed? Fairness: does the error rate differ across groups? A single accuracy number can hide this completely. Consequence: who is affected by a wrong answer, and can they appeal it? And remember, it was publicly available answers a legal question, not an ethical one.
67: What does this mean practically for your exploration? Six steps. One, count before you model: tabulate rows per group, because tiny subgroups cannot support a reliable claim about themselves. Two, split every summary by group, because one overall accuracy or mean can hide two very different stories. Three, check missingness by group: if data is missing more often for one group, dropping those rows removes that group. Four, ask where the labels came from: who decided, using what rule, and were they consistent? Five, write down what you did, a short datasheet with the source, collection method, known gaps and exclusions. Six, say what the data cannot answer. The most useful sentence in many reports begins: this dataset does not tell us.
68: Remember this much. Numbers in, responsibility out. An image is a grid of brightness values, and colour adds a third axis. Audio is one long list of amplitudes, and becomes an image once you compute a spectrogram. Every extra feature multiplies the space to be covered, so data thins out fast. Bias enters at collection and labelling, long before any model is trained. Split by group, count the rows, and write down what the data cannot say. Next: the tools that make high dimensions manageable.
